At MacArthur Park, aid workers face an endless cycle of overdoses — and a system that can’t keep up
Service workers reversing overdoses and connecting people to housing say recent drug enforcement is undoing years of trust.
Jordan Rynning
has reported from MacArthur Park since early 2025, tracking enforcement and talking to people at the park about what they're experiencing.
Published October 30, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT
From left, Immanuel Camacho, Aurora Morales, Joseph Cathey and Angel Borjas of the Homeless Health Care Los Angeles overdose response team patrol the park on Nov. 3, 2025.
Jordan Rynning
LAist)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Listen
3:56
At MacArthur Park, aid workers focus on giving people 'just one more day'
The cycle of reviving drug users from the "fentanyl fold" happens over and over. Jordan Rynning got a firsthand look at what it takes to keep people alive in the park.
Aurora Morales was walking through an alley near MacArthur Park on Nov. 3, 2025, when she spotted something hidden behind a small group of people.
“There’s a guy,” Morales called out to her teammate, Angel Borjas. “He’s behind his wheelchair. He’s really hard to see.”
The man was squatted down and bent over at the waist, his forehead nearly touching the ground. For the Homeless Health Care L.A. overdose response team out that day, it was a familiar pose and a common sign of opioid use — known as "riding" or the "fentanyl fold."
The man bent over in front of them was behind buildings off Alvarado Street. It’s known as "Fentanyl Alley" and is half a block from MacArthur Park, where the team patrols every day. Fentanyl has devastated the area.
At the scene, team members gave the man an oxygen mask to breathe into. They explained to me how oxygen counteracts an often-deadly effect of fentanyl called respiratory depression — when the person's brain stops telling their body to breathe.
When the man regained his composure, he introduced himself as Sal. He told me he was feeling much better. He had recently returned to the park after his friends were concerned about his health and called LAFD paramedics, who took him to a hospital.
He seemed unfazed by his latest close call. “I’m just getting started, man!” Sal told me.
Sponsored message
Aid workers handed Sal a package of naloxone, an overdose-reversing drug also known by the brand name Narcan. One of the aid workers, Joseph Cathey, told him the team would be back around to check on him.
A note on sources
Some of the people who spoke to me for this series were involved in illegal activities, did not have legal U.S. residency status or feared for their safety if they talked to a reporter. In some cases, people agreed to use a first name or nickname to speak more openly about their situations. Others would only talk to me on the condition that they remain anonymous. I only used information from anonymous sources that was corroborated by others.
Had the service workers not been there, Morales said, he would have overdosed.
"Now he's up, he's breathing, he's talking." Morales said. "We got to prolong his life just one more day."
They saved a man’s life that morning — and they said it was a slow day.
MacArthur Park, once a destination for the most affluent Angelenos, has become a symbol of the opioid overdose epidemic that has torn across the U.S. in recent years.
The area is also recovering from a 2023 spike in violent crime — though still second only to Skid Row as the most violent place in L.A., according to an LAist analysis of LAPD crime data. Daily dangers at the park have left many afraid to go.
Sponsored message
In an attempt to save lives, local officials have contracted a wide range of services to serve MacArthur Park, including free medical programs and gang violence reduction teams. Community organizations have also rallied to the area to regularly bring food, clothing and other necessities for people in need.
The high level of assistance creates tension between people who view the help as compassionate and others who see it as enabling drug use and criminal activity. Those in favor of more enforcement argue that local government leaders should focus on cracking down on crime, not making it easier for people to use drugs around the park.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli points toward MacArthur Park while speaking at a press conference after a drug enforcement operation there on May 6, 2026. “In my opinion, [needle exchange programs] make it worse,” Essayli told reporters. “You got these black Jeeps that drive around doing harm reduction, which means they're handing out clean needles, making it easier to sell drugs.”
Jordan Rynning
LAist)
Mehmet Oz, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services administrator, was also at the press conference, and criticized local government leaders for “farming homelessness” by making it easy to do drugs near the park. “This is a fundamental disagreement that I think we have in America,” Oz said. “Giving people who are addicted what they need [to use drugs] doesn't free them.”
Jordan Rynning
LAist)
As Mayor Karen Bass debated challengers Nithya Raman and Spencer Pratt the same night as the May 6 raid, she said she would end the city’s needle exchange program, which has provided clean needles across the city since it was implemented to prevent the spread of AIDS/HIV in 1996. Bass reaffirmed that she did not support the program during a separate mayoral forum on Oct. 15. Nithya Raman, who advanced to the general election against Bass, has said she would not end the program.

Cal State LA wants memorabilia from your gig-going days for its underground music archive
Bring photos, fliers and ticket stubs shows to the college on Thursday Nov. 5.
Right around the year 2000, there was a club night in Hollywood called Clockwork Orange. Fans of The Smiths, Depeche Mode, Bauhaus and other bands came for the DJ’s mix of their favorite songs but also for a vibe that welcomed people regardless of race, ethnicity or sexual and gender identity.
“I was a pretty shy person, and so that was a place where I could sort of be myself and express myself,” said Azalea Camacho, a regular there in those days.
She had just graduated from Workman High School in the City of Industry and was also clubbing at rockabilly music nights in Rosemead and goth club nights in downtown L.A.
Camacho said there was lots of memorabilia from those times, such as photos taken in and outside the clubs, ticket stubs and promotional fliers. They're the physical remnants of those supportive communities built around music and enjoyment, but many of them languish in shoeboxes and storage units, at risk of being lost — along with the memories attached to them.
Cal State LA has hosted Sounds of the Underground Archive for the last four years. It's an opportunity for people to donate their underground music scene memorabilia.
Courtesy Special Collections and Archives, University Library, California State University, Los Angeles)
“I think the danger is maybe those stories are not being told, or people don't know about the story,” she said.
Sponsored message
Keeping stories alive
More than two decades later, Camacho is now in a position to make sure those stories are kept alive. She’s head of special collections and archives at the university library at California State University, Los Angeles.
Four years ago, she and library staff created an annual day for area residents to donate or digitize memorabilia for their Sounds of the Underground Archive. This year it's on Thursday, Nov. 5. They’ll accept physical donations, but they’ll also have a scanner to digitize printed material, so people can keep items that are precious to them.
SOUNDS OF THE UNDERGROUND ARCHIVE
Date: Thursday, Nov. 5
Time: 2 p.m. – 5 p.m.
Location: Cal State LA Library Community Room, 5151 State University Drive, Los Angeles
Camacho is hoping this year will bring in a bumper amount of memorabilia. It's taken time to get the word out, she said.
“From the actual community archiving day [we’ve collected] maybe 100 or less than 100 items. … It's not a lot,” she said.
She said they're on the lookout for a wide range of mementos, including:
Fliers
Handbills
Zines
Newsletters
Posters
Set lists
Photographs (prints, negatives or digital files)
Cassette tapes, CDs, or vinyl records
Ticket stubs
Wristbands
Band merchandise (stickers, buttons, patches, T-shirts)
DIY press kits or liner notes and correspondence (letters, emails, messages related to music scenes)
Venue or collective ephemera (membership cards, schedules, announcements and more)

Fiona Ng
is LAist's deputy managing editor and leads a team of reporters who explore food, culture, history, events and more.
Published October 30, 2026 at 12:00 PM PDT
The Boulevard, Pasadena's last gay bar, is closing after 45 years.
Fiona Ng
LAist)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Listen
2:52
After four decades, it's last call for Pasadena's only gay bar
Here's Steven Terradot, owner of The Boulevard.
The Boulevard, Pasadena’s last gay bar that has stood witness to the worst years of the AIDS crisis and so much more, is closing after 45 years on Saturday with a farewell bash of drag and karaoke.
“We’ve had weddings. We’ve had funerals. We’ve had college graduations,” said Steven Terradot, owner of The Boulevard, who’s retiring and has put the bar up for sale.
“You always feel welcome,” said David Imai, who first came to the bar in 2012. “This place has a reputation of being the gay Cheers for a reason.”
Come November, what Pasadena loses isn't just a cozy watering hole, but a keeper of its LGBTQ+ past.
“We were more than just a place that sold drinks — or more than a party,” Terradot, 69, said. “I like to think that we had a conscience here, you know?”
Fridays are drag nights at the bar.
Fiona Ng
LAist)
The Boulevard in Pasadena.
Fiona Ng
LAist)
How The Boulevard survived the AIDS crisis
The Boulevard, Terradot said, opened in 1981, when original owners Randy Biggs and partner Carl got a liquor license after buying its predecessor, The Office, a gay beer-and-wine bar.
Sponsored message
At the time, Pasadena had a cluster of queer night spots, Terradot said. Among them: The Vermie’s on Foothill Boulevard; Nardi’s, which became Copa; and The Whistle Stop, near The Office when it was on Colorado Boulevard.
Terradot first set foot inside the newly opened Boulevard in his mid-20s. “I looked both ways to see if anybody saw me come in, because there was a shame and a guilt in those days about who you were,” he said.
The place was packed, filled with people seeking belonging, sex, friendship — even as the AIDS epidemic was becoming full blown. He became a regular, eventually moonlighting as a bartender.
The Boulevard bartender Jamal Glasglow (left) and owner Steven Terradot (right).
Fiona Ng
LAist)
The Boulevard on Foothill Boulevard.
Fiona Ng
LAist)
The Boulevard felt the devastation of HIV.
“I saw it as a young man here,” Terradot said.
The daytime crowd of mostly older gay men, Terradot said, “started dropping like flies and it was scary, it was sad, and you couldn't do anything.”
Sponsored message
Funerals were commonplace at The Boulevard and bar regulars started a fund for those in need.
“All we could do was try to get money for medicine or food or rent because people would get fired, they'd lose their health insurance,” he said.
Farewell and Halloween bash at The Boulevard
Event: Last Call at the Boo-levard! (costumes encouraged)
Where: The Boulevard Bar, 3199 E. Foothill Blvd., Pasadena
When: Saturday, Oct. 31, starting at 7 p.m.
Ages: 21+
To say hi to Steven Terradot, look for the guy with an unlit cigarette dangling between his lips.
Why he bought a struggling bar in 1999
In 1999, Terradot bought The Boulevard, three years after the introduction of the so-called “AIDS cocktail,” which turned HIV into a manageable chronic condition.
At the time, business was slow. The internet was making it easy for LGBTQ+ folks to find each other. And his regulars were going to West Hollywood and Silver Lake to meet new people.
“The first Friday night I owned this bar, we did $200 on the register,” Terradot said.
Sponsored message
But he saw it as a calling of sorts.
“I lost 11 friends during the AIDS epidemic,” he said. “I wanted to do something.”
A new generation finds community
Honey B. Hive hosts Tuesday trans nights at The Boulevard.
Fiona Ng
LAist)
To give the bar a jolt, Terradot started its now-signature karaoke nights. He then made drag a weekly night.
In recent years, The Boulevard has become a place for trans folks to build community, adding trans nights on Tuesdays.
“For a long time I would come to The Boulevard in drag, and I would just pick up a lot of the queens' tips, and that was my way of paying my dues,” said Honey B. Hive, a drag performer.
Sponsored message
Before long, she was anchoring Tuesday trans nights.
“A lot of the San Gabriel Valley comes for Tuesdays,” she said. “People have been coming ever since it started. It feels very familial.”
One last rush, and hope for a buyer
On its final Sunday, after the leather social and before karaoke, Terradot was pitching in behind the bar.
David Imai is a Boulevard regular.
Fiona Ng
LAist)
Business has more than tripled, he said, as old-timers and newcomers flood in after hearing about the closure.
“It does feel like we are losing a resource and a local hangout for those of us living in the San Gabriel Valley,” Imai, the longtime regular, said.
A buyer could still reopen The Boulevard. Terradot said he’s holding out until mid-November for an offer before packing it all up and walking into the sunset.
He hopes someone out there sees the importance of a neighborhood gay bar.
“You still have kids that are lost that come in here, OK? You need to stick a hand out to them,” Terradot said. “So that is the role of the gay bar.”

Appeals court rejects Justice Department request for California to set aside disputed ballots
By Safiyah Riddle | Associated Press
Published October 30, 2026 at 12:48 PM PDT
The U.S. Department of Justice logo is seen on a podium before a press conference, May 6, 2025, at the Justice Department in Washington.
Julia Demaree Nikhinson
Associated Press)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday rejected the Justice Department’s request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election.
The panel’s 2-1 ruling is the latest setback for the Trump administration’s efforts to assert control over state-run elections.
Read the decision
The administration has alleged California sent ballots to some 20,000 people who may not be U.S. citizens. It wants the state to set those ballots aside and not count them until citizenship can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
A district court judge already forcefully denied that request and warned that the Justice Department’s demands could disenfranchise citizens.
“As the district court found — and we discern no clear error — there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system,” the appeals court wrote.
The ruling is the latest in an expansive legal battle between the federal government and the state before Election Day in the midterms Tuesday. Millions of people in California have already voted.
Sponsored message
The majority opinion was authored by Judge Mark J. Bennett, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, and Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden.
The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.
Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. Elections officials have said that processed votes are completely anonymized and can’t be matched back to the voters who submitted them.
The ruling comes during broader federal scrutiny of local elections, with the Trump administration issuing a raft of subpoenas in Alaska in a spoiler-candidate controversy. The Justice Department has also provided a list of alleged noncitizen voters to officials in Washington state.
Outside groups sued for access to the disputed list
Earlier on Friday, a federal judge in Washington ordered the Trump administration to share the disputed list of names with lawyers for the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights and the UCLA Voting Rights Project. They want the list so they can examine who is on the list and assess its impact on eligible voters.
It will be the first time that a nongovernment organization will have the opportunity to evaluate the merits of the list of some 20,000 names.
Sponsored message
Prosecutors with the Trump administration have argued that there is just as much to lose from noncitizens illegally voting, arguing that to tally those votes would dilute the voice of citizens.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra is an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.
The two groups sued the Homeland Security Department in early October to prevent it from using federal immigration data to challenge state voter rolls. The lawsuit cited examples in other states where the federal government’s data has been proven to mistakenly include thousands of citizens. It argued that the data-matching methods risk disenfranchising or deterring citizens from voting. On top of that, plaintiffs argued, the lists could disproportionately target naturalized citizens who are legally entitled to vote.
Another suit seeks to defend election workers
A coalition of unions on Friday also joined the growing list of groups challenging the federal government’s efforts.
The unions, including the A.F.L.-C.I.O. and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, are asking a federal judge to temporarily block the Justice Department from demanding that local officials stop counting ballots and to drop threats to criminally prosecute officials who do not comply with their demands.
The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, Bill Essayli, has warned that “any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy.”
Sponsored message
On Thursday the Associated Press obtained subpoenas issued to election officials in Los Angeles County. The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining the allegations about noncitizen voters. They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted. At least three L.A. County election officials have been asked to appear before a grand jury on Nov. 4, the day after the election.
The lawsuit accuses the Justice Department of issuing threats against election officials that could interfere with their ability to process votes.
It is unclear whether the Justice Department intends to bring criminal charges against anyone. The department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.

One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
The Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office dropped its felony body armor charges against Michael Angel Alvarez on Wednesday. Alvarez was sentenced to time served on a lesser charge — a probation violation. He had served more than 100 days in jail earlier this year while awaiting trial.
Why Alvarez’s arrest made headlines: Alvarez was working as a city-contracted peace ambassador in MacArthur Park when he was arrested by federal agents in May. Federal and county prosecutors each brought felony charges against him, claiming he was in possession of body armor as a violent felon.
Bill Essayli, who leads the U.S. Attorney’s office in L.A., pointed to the case on social media to criticize city officials for allowing taxpayer money to be “shelled out to a convicted gang murderer.”
About his criminal record: Judges in federal and state court have now dismissed prosecutors’ felony charges against Alvarez, after U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang found on Sept. 9 that Alvarez did not have a violent felony conviction. Alvarez was 15 when he committed a gang-related murder. He was tried and convicted as an adult in 2002. After a change in state law increased the age at which minors could be sentenced as adults to 16, Alvarez’s case was sent back to juvenile court, and he was released in 2024. At that point, he had served more than 20 years.
Most serious claims haven’t materialized: Though federal prosecutors made headlines claiming in court documents that Alvarez was “leading a violent street gang, while claiming to be a gang interventionist for the City,” they have not filed charges related to those claims.
About Essayli's role
A federal judge ruled Tuesday, Oct. 7 that Republican Bill Essayli is not legally serving as the top U.S. prosecutor in Los Angeles.
The ruling is the latest roadblock to the Trump administration’s effort to extend handpicked acting U.S. attorneys beyond the 120-day limit set by federal law. The strategy was designed to bypass confirmation by the U.S. Senate — something that generally requires a degree of bipartisan support.
Essayli “is unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States Attorney,” U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright wrote.
The order won’t take effect until the court rules on the government’s motion for a stay pending appeal. Essayli said he doesn’t agree with the court’s order. He said the president and Attorney General “have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department.”
Read more
— Associated Press

LA coastal flooding breaks record set in 1983 — with more almost certainly ahead
Kevin Tidmarsh
is a producer for LAist, covering news and culture. He’s been an audio/web journalist for about a decade.
Published October 30, 2026 at 4:21 PM PDT
Tidewaters flood businesses and homes along Pacific Coast Highway in Orange County's Sunset Beach.
Robert Gauthier
Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Listen
0:45
How much more coastal flooding does SoCal have in store?
Forecasters can't put an exact number on how many more days of coastal flooding to expect this year, but they're already watching for upcoming king tide events.
Los Angeles has handily broken its record for most days of coastal flooding in a year. And that’s without including October in the tally and with a wet El Niño winter ahead — a worrying sign for coastal homes and infrastructure.
Researchers can’t yet project how many more days of flooding we’ll have in 2026 — but we’re already well ahead of what the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s models had forecast up to this point.
NOAA oceanographer Karen Kavanaugh said models had predicted three to six flood days between May 2026 and April 2027. Those models took El Niño and sea level rise into account. She said that there have already been nine flood days in that window and added that the 12 flood days so far in the calendar year are “abnormally high.”
The number of days of coastal flooding observed at NOAA’s tide gauge in San Pedro is the highest recorded since observations started being taken in 1923. The previous record was set at nine in 1983, during another El Niño event.
Preparing for El Niño
How to prepare your home for El Niño’s extreme weather
Now’s the time to take steps to protect your home from heavy rain, flooding and landslides that could come with this year’s potentially historic El Niño season.
With a strong El Niño expected in SoCal, should you consider flood insurance?
The weather pattern doesn’t guarantee flooding here, but now could be a good time to consider flood insurance, which is not included in most homeowners or renters policies.
SoCal drivers, get your car ready for El Niño's road hazards
El Niño’s signature heavy rains could make driving more risky than usual. Make sure your car is safe now, before extreme weather hits.
When might we see more flooding?
Kavanaugh couldn’t say with certainty when flooding might occur, but noted that high-risk times ahead coincide with Thanksgiving and Christmas. Around then, the moon will be at its closest point to the Earth. The stronger gravitational pull from the moon causes what are commonly known as king tides, a nonscientific term for the highest predicted tides of the year.
Sponsored message
In addition to these factors, the wide range of events affecting our tides this year, including storms, climate change, El Niño and related Kelvin waves, could very well cause other flooding events or cause the existing ones to become stronger.
Kavanaugh said a combination of factors — specifically Kelvin waves and astronomical high tides — was exactly what was responsible for the flooding seen this week.
“That could happen, perhaps, again in November and December if we have another pulse of a Kelvin wave,” Kavanaugh said.
Flooding inundated coastal communities around Southern California this week, including Orange County's Sunset Beach.
Robert Gauthier
Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
How high will the tides be?
Unfortunately, Kavanaugh said, there’s no way to predict the severity of upcoming king tide events at this moment in time.
“But as we move closer to an event, there are good models that the National Weather Service uses to forecast flooding,” she added. “But they need it to be within seven days, sometimes shorter timelines.”
Sponsored message
High tide resources
These NOAA resources can help you plan for and monitor high tide events:
Monthly high tide flooding outlook
Annual high tide flooding outlook
NOAA’s real-time coastal inundation dashboard
How to prepare for high tide conditions
Kavanaugh recommended keeping an eye on National Weather Service reports for the latest information and predictions. (There are separate pages for Los Angeles and Orange counties.)
Kavanaugh stressed that, given this year's unpredictability so far, people should be as prepared as possible.
“It's an unusual type of phenomenon to plan for for some communities,” she said. “We're used to planning for a big storm, maybe, and flooding from that, but not planning for, ‘Oh, it's gonna be beautiful sunny weather, and also you might have flooding on the roads.’”
Kavanaugh also recommended paying close attention to local emergency officials’ guidance and being mindful not to park cars in low-lying areas that could end up being inundated.
“If [local officials are] asking you to get sandbags or things like that, keep those sandbags because you might need them again in a few weeks,” she said.

LA approves initial $5 million to help Boyle Heights residents, businesses recover from Lineage fire
By Laura Anaya-Morga | Boyle Heights Beat
Published October 30, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT
The Lineage warehouse in Boyle Heights on Aug. 31, 2026.
Brian Feinzimer
The LA Local)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
The Los Angeles City Council approved the transfer of $5 million Wednesday to support residents and businesses affected by the Lineage warehouse fire, part of a $10.5 million recovery package proposed by Councilmember Ysabel Jurado.
Households and businesses will soon be able to apply to receive assistance through a program established by the city’s Community Investment Department (CID). A timeline on when the applications will open or when grants will be provided was not immediately available.
A significant portion of the initial funding will go toward improving sanitation services near Lineage, including paying for workers’ overtime salaries to enhance pressure washing, bulky item pickup and to respond to illegal dumping.
Jurado addressed the council at Wednesday’s meeting, describing how the June fire had impacted residents’ health, livelihoods and peace of mind.
“The emergency is still ongoing, and it won’t end until the city can fulfill the long-term commitment we made with them to set a new bar for the level of care that the Eastside deserves. The funding that we can advance today is a milestone in turning that commitment, the promise that Boyle Heights can once again believe in its own future, into action,” Jurado said.
Months after the fire, residents reported dealing with exorbitant utility bills caused by running air purifiers and air conditioners over the summer. Some residents told Boyle Heights Beat that they lost work due to the fire and that support from Lineage, the city and county in the immediate aftermath was not enough.
Here’s how the initial $5 million breaks down:
$2.5 million in direct financial assistance will go to more than 100 qualifying Boyle Heights businesses and Lineage workers in ZIP codes 90033, 90032, and 90063.
Qualified businesses with fewer than 6 employees will be eligible to receive $2,500 per month for six months.
Qualified businesses with 6 or more employees will be eligible to receive $5,000 per month for six months.
LA City residents employed by Lineage and experiencing economic hardship because of the fire will be eligible to receive $2,000 per month for six months.
$1.8 million in direct financial awards will go toward qualifying Boyle Heights households that were affected by the fire.
$664,460 will go toward funding supplies and overtime salaries for pressure washing, bulky item pickup, and illegal dumping responses in Boyle Heights through the end of the current fiscal year on June 30, 2027.
The initial $5 million from the city’s unappropriated balance will go to L.A. Sanitation and CID. The additional proposed $5.5 million will come from Measure A funding to further support residents, according to Jurado’s office.
Sponsored message
What we still don’t know:
It is still unclear when the application will open, how soon grants will be provided and how many residents and businesses will be chosen to receive financial relief. It is also unclear how soon L.A. Sanitation will begin additional cleanup near Lineage. Boyle Heights Beat has reached out to the CID with those questions and will update this story when we find out more.
